lines.text: therapist prescribed certain BCRL self-care modali-
ties that may result in underreporting. Furthermore,
participants may have also forgotten the frequency in
which their lymphedema therapist recommended
certain BCRL self-care activities to be undertaken. All
participants were required to attend a 1-hr educa-
tional lecture entitled the BLymphedema Education
Session[ that was based on material from the Na-
tional Lymphedema Network. This educational ses-
sion was taught by the PAL principal investigator
(Schmitz) to ensure that all participants had a com-
parable understanding of lymphedema self-care
methods while in the PAL trial. However, the au-
thors did not collect information that allowed them
to quantify the level of BCRL self-care education or
skill in completing the prescribed BCRL self-care
activities. Therefore, the authors’ null findings may
reflect poor or inappropriate use of the prescribed
modalities because of insufficient patient education,
rather than poor subject adherence to the BCRL self-
care modalities.
Additional limitations to the exploratory analysis
include the limited number of observed outcomes.
The small sample size of outcomes precluded the ex-
amination of adherence to individual BCRL modalities
and BCRL outcomes. The small sample size also pre-
cluded the exploration of specific demographic and
clinical subgroups. When the authors conducted
sensitivity analyses treating the outcome variables
(i.e., volumetry, circumference measures, etc.) as
continuous measures in multivariable-adjusted re-
gression models, their results were similar to one
another. Adjustment for randomized group assign-
ment did not influence the study findings. The au-
thors’ previous report demonstrated that randomized
group did not influence BCRL self-care practices
during the 12-mo study.
The ability for those with BCRL to adequately
adhere to BCRL self-care has been a concern for
more than a decade.
A previous study determined
that noncompliance with BCRL bandaging and
compression garment use were risk factors for in-
creased arm volume 1 yr after receiving complete
decongestive therapy.
Poor BCRL self-care com-
pliance to phase II decongestive activities after re-
ceiving phase I complete decongestive therapy has
resulted in failure rates of 38%, 53%, and 65% at 1,
2, and 4 yrs, respectively.
Restricting the authors’
analyses to only include phase II complete decon-
gestive activities, their conclusions did not change.
Nonetheless, these data suggest that new strategies
and methods to maintain arm health are needed
among BrCa survivors with BCRL.
The PAL trial demonstrated that twice-weekly
weight lifting reduced the need for therapist-defined
BCRL treatment by 53% (P = 0.04).
